title: First Motion: Driving a Robot in a Straight Line

questions.question: What three numbers make up a pose?
options: Position along x, position along y, and the heading angle
Left wheel speed, right wheel speed, and time
Distance, speed, and acceleration
Latitude, longitude, and altitude
questions.explanation: A pose is where the robot is and which way it faces. For a robot on a flat floor that is x, y and theta.

questions.question: Both wheels turn at 1.0 metres per second. What does the robot do?
options: Drives straight forward at 1.0 metres per second
Spins in place
Curves to the left
Stays still because the speeds cancel
questions.explanation: Forward speed is the average of the two, which is 1.0. Turn rate comes from the difference, which is zero, so there is no rotation.

questions.question: Why is the turn rate divided by the wheel base rather than multiplied?
options: Wheels further apart turn more slowly for the same speed difference
Because the wheel base is always smaller than one
To convert metres into radians
To keep the result positive
questions.explanation: A wide robot needs a bigger speed difference to achieve the same turn rate, so the base appears in the denominator.

questions.question: The robot faces along the y axis and drives forward, but your code moves it along x. What is wrong?
options: Sine and cosine are swapped
The time step is too large
The wheel base is wrong
The angle was not wrapped
questions.explanation: Cosine of theta gives the x component of a direction and sine gives the y component. Swapping them rotates all motion by ninety degrees.

questions.question: Why must the heading be wrapped back into minus pi to pi?
options: Otherwise it grows without limit and headings can no longer be compared
Because sine and cosine reject large inputs
Because the robot cannot physically turn more than once
To stop the value overflowing its type
questions.explanation: The angle still points the right way, but comparing 401.2 radians with 0.1 radians gives a nonsense difference. Wrapping keeps headings comparable.

questions.question: This model assumes the robot travels in a straight line during each time step. Why is that acceptable?
options: With small enough time steps the error is tiny, and it is what real robots use
Because robots only ever drive in straight lines
Because the arc version is impossible to compute
Because the error cancels out over time
questions.explanation: It is a deliberate approximation. The error shrinks with the time step, and lesson 13 measures it against the exact arc form.
